acceptance_criteria.criterion: The `ProvisioningTools` factory arm no longer uses `GetRequiredService<ProvisioningToolsViewModel>()`.
`AddTransient<ProvisioningToolsViewModel>()` is absent from the DI registrations.

summary: Removed `builder.Services.AddTransient<ProvisioningToolsViewModel>()` from the DI registrations in Program.cs.

Changed the ProvisioningTools factory arm in the ShellViewModel singleton factory to construct ProvisioningToolsViewModel directly via its two-argument constructor, passing the `provisioner` local variable and an `onComplete` callback that calls `lazyShell!.AdvanceToConnecting()`.
Added `using System.Diagnostics;` to support `Debug.Assert` in the callback.
Build: 0 errors, 0 warnings. Tests: 344 passed, 0 failed.

comments.note: No observations — code in the touched files is clean and consistent. The inline lambda in the switch arm is intentionally compact per the existing style of the other factory arms.

summary: All 4 acceptance criteria verified through code inspection and build/test execution.
AC1: dotnet build succeeds — 0 errors, 0 warnings.
AC2: ProvisioningTools factory arm uses `new ProvisioningToolsViewModel(provisioner, onComplete: ...)` — no GetRequiredService call.
AC3: No `AddTransient<ProvisioningToolsViewModel>()` found anywhere in the codebase.
AC4: `lazyShell!.AdvanceToConnecting()` is wired as the onComplete callback in the lambda.
Regression: 345 passed, 5 skipped, 0 failed across all three test assemblies.

Edge-case analysis: (1) lazyShell null-before-assign timing is safe — StartAsync() is called after the ShellViewModel constructor returns, so lazyShell is always assigned before any async continuation fires; (2) double-callback via Retry is blocked because CanRetry() requires Error != null, which is null on the success path.

comments.note: The `Debug.Assert(lazyShell is not null)` guard before `lazyShell!.AdvanceToConnecting()` is appropriate as a debug-mode safety net. In release builds the assert is elided but the null-forgiving operator still produces correct behaviour because the timing guarantees ensure lazyShell is always assigned before the callback fires.
No regressions found. Code is clean and consistent with the rest of the factory arm pattern in Program.cs.

summary: WP-005 passes code review. The implementation in Program.cs is correct, minimal, and fully consistent with the existing factory-arm style.
AC1-4 all met and previously verified by QA.
The onComplete callback fires only on the success path (after EnsureAsync returns without throwing); cancel and exception paths do not invoke it — correct per ProvisioningToolsViewModel contract.

AdvanceToConnecting() called from a ThreadPool thread is consistent with the existing ShellViewModel pattern where ConnectAsync, LogOnAsync, and SetPasswordAsync all use ConfigureAwait(false) then call Transition() from the pool.

Debug.Assert(lazyShell is not null) + ! null-forgiving operator pattern is appropriate — the timing guarantee (lazyShell assigned before StartAsync runs) makes the assert accurate in debug builds and the forgiving operator safe in release builds.
ShellViewModel.ProvisionAsync() being dead production code is a deliberate, documented decision (plan.md line 75) to preserve existing unit-test coverage — not rework-worthy technical debt.
One documentation-forward item raised: README.md still describes ProvisionAsync() as the orchestration entry point for ProvisioningTools → Connecting; needs updating to reflect callback-based wiring.
No Fix-Forward edits applied; no blocking issues found.

comments.note: No blocking or fix-forward issues found. Code is clean and consistent with the existing factory-arm pattern in Program.cs.
